overview.statement: Costa Rica's health system is public and organised as a National Health System that links two bodies: the Costa Rican Social Security Fund (CCSS), which runs both the health insurance and the disability, old-age and death pension insurance and also delivers care, and the Ministry of Health, which acts as the sector's steward.

locator.section: Caracterización del sistema de salud costarricense

overview.statement: Care is delivered through three integrated networks organised by territory and by level of complexity, made up of peripheral, regional and national clinics and hospitals; basic comprehensive health care teams (EBAIS) are the point of entry and the link with communities.

locator.section: Caracterización del sistema de salud costarricense

overview.statement: The CCSS, set up in 1941, is the main social insurance institution: it provides medical care together with sickness, maternity, old-age and invalidity benefits to its direct members, and for health care it can also cover their dependants. It is financed by contributions from employers, workers and the State.

A 2026 OECD, IDB and World Bank report names Costa Rica, with Chile, Colombia and Uruguay, as one of the few Latin American countries whose programmes bring the whole population into a single system with cross-subsidies, while noting that benefits and access in such systems still vary between rural and urban areas and between contributors and fully subsidised people.

locator.section: Chapter 2: Inequalities in health and health care

overview.statement: As part of the primary care reforms, all public-sector health care, from primary to tertiary, was moved to the CCSS alone instead of being provided by both the Ministry of Health and the CCSS, and the ministry was given responsibility for stewardship of the system.

locator.table: Table 3: Reforms identified for Costa Rica's PHC model, row 'Governance restructuring'

financing.statement: Health insurance (the CCSS's Seguro de Enfermedad y Maternidad, SEM) is funded by payroll contributions of 9.25% of wages paid by employers and 5.5% paid by employees, 14.75% in total, according to an OECD table sourced to the CCSS (2025).

locator.table: Table 8.4: Payroll-based contributions in Costa Rica, by entity of destination (row SEM/Health: employer, employee, total)

financing.statement: The State adds its own contribution of 0.25% to the health insurance scheme (and 1.91% to the contributory pension fund); each year the Ministry of Finance sets aside funds in the national budget that are then transferred to the CCSS.

The State also pays for several health programmes created by legislation, such as vaccination, in vitro fertilisation, insurance cover for vulnerable groups and smoking cessation, financing them from taxes or borrowing.

Contributions are charged on a minimum base: in 2023 the floor below which no salaried worker could contribute was set at US$603 for health care (US$564 for pensions), and in 2022 the CCSS board lowered the minimum contributory income for independent workers to US$283.

Contribution to the health insurance is compulsory for all workers. For employees it is shared three ways, by employers, workers and the State; for self-employed and voluntary members it is shared two ways, by the worker and the State. Pensioners' contributions and specific State-funded programmes complete the scheme.

In the July 2025 national household survey, 11.7% of people were insured through the State (seguro por el Estado), a share that reached 40.7% among people who were poor by both the income-poverty line and the multidimensional poverty index.

locator.table: Cuadro 4.12 (households and people by poverty status, July 2025; excludes domestic workers and pensioners living in the household); row 'Porcentaje de personas con seguro por el Estado'; columns in order: total country, not poor by either measure, poor by income line, poor by multidimensional index, poor by both

financing.statement: Public spending makes up 70% of total health spending.

locator.section: Caracterización del sistema de salud costarricense

financing.statement: Citing World Bank data, the OECD puts out-of-pocket payments at 22.3% of current health expenditure, below the Latin American regional average of 28.3%; on this basis it describes financial protection for health care as high.

locator.section: 8.3.1 Overview of existing systems (coverage and financial protection)

financing.statement: Taken together, payroll contributions to all bodies come to about 37% of wages; employers pay 72% of this (26.5% of wages) and workers 28% (10.5%), and 64.8% of the total goes to the CCSS for health insurance and contributory pensions.
Employers' payroll charges, at 21% of labour costs in 2024, are higher than in the average OECD country.

locator.figure: Figure 8.8: Employer contributions, % of labour costs, 2024

financing.statement: The OECD estimates that cutting the employer health-insurance contribution rate by one percentage point would reduce health revenues by the equivalent of 0.4% of GDP.

locator.section: 8.5.2 Reducing employers' contributions to the CCSS

covered.statement: By law, the whole population has access to emergency services, and contributory health insurance covers about 89% of the population (OECD, 2025).
An OECD estimate based on the 2024 national household survey puts the share of the population with social health insurance at 90.2%.

locator.table: Table 8.3: Social protection coverage rates, by group, 2024

covered.statement: According to the 2024 National Household Survey, 10% of people nationally had no health insurance, rising to 11% in rural areas.

locator.section: Caracterización del sistema de salud costarricense

covered.statement: Non-contributory forms of coverage, such as the family benefit insurance, give economically dependent close relatives of directly insured people access to health care.

locator.section: Brecha entre la cobertura asegurada y la contributiva

covered.statement: Social security cannot refuse care to anyone who needs it, regardless of insurance status, although in principle it is supposed to charge uninsured people for the cost of that care.

locator.section: Brecha entre la cobertura asegurada y la contributiva

covered.statement: Under the primary care reform, each household was assigned to a multidisciplinary team (EBAIS) purely according to where it lives, with about 4,000 people per team.

locator.table: Table 3: Reforms identified for Costa Rica's PHC model, row 'Geographic empanelment'

covered.statement: Which medicines the CCSS covers is set by its Official Medicines List, compiled by expert doctors and pharmacists against criteria that include efficacy, safety, the ratio of costs to benefits, the effect on the system's financial sustainability, and whether all population groups can obtain and properly use the medicine.

locator.section: Effects of the reform on resource allocation

covered.statement: The Constitution contains no explicit right to health, but the Constitutional Chamber of the Supreme Court (Sala IV) has derived one from the right to life (article 21), the right to social security (article 73) and international human rights treaties; this right covers public and preventive health services as well as medical care.
The General Health Law of 1974 and the solidarity-based social security model establish a universal right to health care.

locator.section: Propuesta teórica para el abordaje de las listas y los tiempos de espera

covered.statement: In the public system most people with diabetes are treated in primary care, and the diabetes medicines available are limited to sulphonylureas, metformin and human insulins; referral to specialists and nutritional counselling exist but usually involve long waiting lists (2023 review).

cost_sharing.statement: In the 2026 OECD/IDB/World Bank survey, Costa Rica named 'Insurance from the State' (Seguro por el Estado) as the channel through which people without sufficient income are insured, with the State paying for their cover.
Apart from contributions, the health insurance has small revenues such as interest, rents and the sale of services to people without insurance, who have to pay for the care they receive.

locator.section: Esquema de financiamiento: desaceleración de los ingresos por contribuciones

additional_care.statement: The private sector is concentrated in the Greater Metropolitan Area and is financed mainly through out-of-pocket payments.

locator.section: Caracterización del sistema de salud costarricense

additional_care.statement: Only a small share of patients have private health insurance, bought individually or received as a job benefit; cover varies and usually involves a co-payment of about 20% for medicines and medical care (2023 review).
With private insurance, patients usually pay the provider first and then claim reimbursement from the insurer, which adds to their financial burden.
Newer diabetes medicines are available in the private sector, but most of the cost is paid out of pocket, which limits access to them.

access.statement: CCSS records show the number of people on waiting lists grew between 2019 and 2024: from 438,599 to 695,328 for outpatient procedures (58.5% more), from 121,270 to 185,845 for surgery (53.2% more) and from 255,672 to 322,901 for specialist outpatient consultations (37% more).

locator.section: Caracterización de las personas en listas de espera

access.statement: In 2024 the average wait for a new specialist outpatient appointment was 466 days, 13% longer than in 2020.

locator.table: Tabla 1: Perfil de los tiempos de espera en Costa Rica (2024 average days; change 2020-2024)

access.statement: In 2024 the average wait was 137 days for outpatient medical procedures (50% longer than in 2020) and 424 days for surgical procedures (26% longer).

locator.table: Tabla 1: Perfil de los tiempos de espera en Costa Rica (2024 average days; change 2020-2024)

access.statement: Waits for specialist outpatient appointments differed widely by province in 2024, from an average of 262 days in Puntarenas to 655 days in Alajuela.

locator.table: Tabla 1: Perfil de los tiempos de espera en Costa Rica, specialist outpatient consultation by province (2024 average days; change 2020-2024)

access.statement: The CCSS responds to waiting lists mainly with extra 'production' sessions outside normal working hours, yet operating theatres are used for only 63% of regular working hours, while the number of people on waiting lists grew by 7% a year on average.
Priority on a waiting list is set by the treating doctor when demand exceeds the network's immediate capacity, provided the condition can wait without risk to life.

locator.section: Caracterización de las personas en listas de espera

access.statement: Seven in ten people (70%) said they were satisfied with the availability of good-quality health care, compared with 64% on average across the OECD.
Costa Rica has 1.1 hospital beds per 1,000 people (OECD average 4.2) and 7 CT scanners, MRI units and PET scanners per million people (OECD average 51).
Costa Rica trains the fewest new doctors among the Latin American countries compared, 4.3 medical graduates per 100,000 people, against a LAC10 average of 12.8 and an OECD average of 14.5.

outcomes.statement: Life expectancy in Costa Rica was 81 years, 0.1 years below the OECD average.
Preventable mortality was 147 deaths per 100,000 people (OECD average 145) and treatable mortality 94 per 100,000 (OECD average 77).
99% of eligible children were vaccinated against diphtheria, tetanus and pertussis, above the OECD average.

In 2023 total avoidable mortality was around 200 deaths per 100,000 people in Costa Rica, against 297 across Latin America and the Caribbean and 162 across the OECD; Costa Rica's treatable mortality (184 per 100,000 men, 66 per 100,000 women) is among the lowest in the region.
Age- and sex-standardised 30-day in-hospital mortality after a heart attack was 6.8% in Costa Rica, close to the OECD average of 6.5%.

locator.section: Chapter 7: In-hospital mortality following AMI and stroke

outcomes.statement: In the GBD 2019 study, Costa Rica's Healthcare Access and Quality (HAQ) Index score for ages 0-74 was 64.7 (95% uncertainty interval 60.4-68.6) in 2019, 11.7 points higher than in 1990.

locator.table: Table: HAQ Index estimates by location; row values in order: 2019 overall (0-74 years), young (0-14), working (15-64), post-working (65-74), then absolute change 1990-2019 for the same four groups

outcomes.statement: In 2018 life expectancy in Costa Rica was 80 years, slightly above the 79.5-year average of countries with 'very high' human development and about 4 years above the 76-year average of the 'high' group in which Costa Rica is ranked.

costs.statement: Costa Rica spends US$1,935 per person on health (USD PPP), against an OECD average of US$5,967, equal to 6.8% of GDP compared with an OECD average of 9.3%.

The OECD says the health sector must shore up the CCSS's financial sustainability, as a recent actuarial assessment highlighted, while delivering adequate services and improving efficiency and cost control.

locator.section: 8.3.1 Overview of existing systems (coverage and financial protection)

what_works.statement: Costa Rica had 161 avoidable hospital admissions per 100,000 people, well below the OECD average of 473.
Costa Rica has long been seen as a model of primary health care among low- and middle-income countries; it reformed primary care in 1994 around basic integrated health care teams.

A study based on 39 key-informant interviews found that Costa Rica carried out its primary care reforms through strong leadership, a compelling vision and deliberate strategies: building on existing knowledge, resources and infrastructure, bringing key stakeholders together and engaging closely with communities.

A Healthcare Delivery Performance Index ranks the country's 106 Health Areas on 15 quality indicators; Health Area Directors use it to start quality improvement work, and the ranking motivates providers without financial incentives.

Public health resources seem to be distributed in favour of the poor: the poorest groups make the most use of public services, and the poorest fifth of the population receives 30% of government health spending.

locator.section: Effects of the reform on resource allocation

what_works.statement: The 2026 OECD/IDB/World Bank report cites Costa Rica's single digital health record, EDUS, as an example of digital access for patients.

problems.statement: The authors conclude that waiting lists rise and fall with the availability of extra budget, even with the same installed capacity, a cyclical pattern that does not resolve them in a lasting way and points to weaknesses in planning, governance and operational continuity.

The CCSS's way of prioritising waiting lists is only weakly aligned with the models examined by the OECD and the IDB, which weigh clinical need and time waited together and add criteria such as severity, urgency, equity and social factors.

locator.section: Caracterización de las personas en listas de espera

problems.statement: In July 2025, 21.3% of poor people had no formal health insurance, compared with 6.0% of people who were not poor by either measure.

locator.section: Características de los hogares en situación de pobreza

problems.statement: Only 22% of women in Costa Rica were screened for breast cancer, compared with an OECD average of 55%.
Costa Rica ranks among the four OECD countries with the lowest doctor productivity, measured as medical visits per doctor.

locator.section: 8.3.1 Overview of existing systems (coverage and financial protection)

problems.statement: Even after the court's 2014 reform, low-priority and experimental medicines made up nearly two-thirds of successful lawsuits for medicines and, by the authors' estimate, more than nine-tenths of the spending on approved claims.

locator.section: Effects of the reform on resource allocation

problems.statement: Court orders are estimated to account for 9% of the CCSS's total medicine spending.
Costa Rica reported to the 2026 OECD/IDB/World Bank survey that it does not measure patient experience at all.
Costa Rica reported that its clinical practice guidelines, including those for cancer and cardiovascular disease, are not regularly updated.
30-day in-hospital mortality after ischaemic stroke was 15.3% in Costa Rica, markedly higher than the OECD average of 8.7%.

locator.section: Chapter 7: In-hospital mortality following AMI and stroke

problems.statement: Social protection, including CCSS health insurance, relies heavily on high payroll contributions, which the OECD identifies as a barrier to formal employment.

reforms.statement: In 2014, with World Bank support, the Constitutional Chamber started a joint programme with the Cochrane Collaboration: instead of mostly accepting the treating doctor's evidence, the court can refer medicine claims to forensic clinics, where a doctor examines the patient and checks the prescribed drug against Cochrane evidence.
The success rate of lawsuits for medicines at the Constitutional Chamber rose from 57.9% of 192 cases in 2008, before the reform, to 76.6% of 128 cases in 2016, after it.

locator.table: Table 3: Success rate of litigation for the provision of medicine, 2008 and 2016

reforms.statement: In 2022 the CCSS board lowered the minimum contributory income for independent workers, setting it at US$283.

To widen digital access, the Ministry of Health created a Virtual Office, piloted kiosks in health areas, issued a decree regulating teleconsultation and began work on digital literacy (as reported in 2026).
In the 1990s Costa Rica carried out three key primary care reforms: restructuring governance, assigning the population to teams by geography, and creating multidisciplinary teams.

The reforms followed the 1980s recession, when an IMF and World Bank structural adjustment programme led Costa Rica to cut public employment and health and social services, after which problems such as less safe drinking water, undernourished children and a measles outbreak appeared.

After the reform, claims for medicines made up a smaller share of all amparo (constitutional protection) cases at the Constitutional Chamber: 128 of 15,782 cases (0.8%) in 2016, against 192 of 16,345 (1.2%) in 2008.

locator.table: Table 4: Litigation for the provision of medicine, 2008 and 2016

us_lessons.statement: The authors of a study of how Costa Rica implemented its primary care reforms say its specific strategies offer concrete lessons for other countries working to strengthen primary health care.

A Health Affairs case study concludes that, for countries pursuing high-quality universal coverage, Costa Rica's experience shows both what kinds of primary care reform are needed and how such reforms can be put in place.

A study of primary care data use concludes that Costa Rica's experience with collecting, analysing and using data for quality improvement holds lessons for primary care in other public-sector systems.
